On his first day as project lead at a Mumbai software firm, Tarun didn't start with tasks. He started with a date.
The client demo was on 20 September. He wrote it in red on the office whiteboard. Then he counted back. Integration testing needed a fortnight, so it began 6 September. Coding had to finish before that, so 5 September. Design had to be signed off by 10 August to leave enough coding time.
His teammate Mridul watched. "You're planning backwards."
"The demo won't move," Tarun said. "Everything else has to fit behind it."
By lunch he had built a shared calendar with each deadline marked, and sent it to the whole team. In the afternoon meeting he put it on the screen. "This is the one calendar we all look at."
Mridul pointed at 6 September. "So if design slips, testing gets squeezed?"
"Exactly. That's why design has the earliest deadline."

I'm Divyansh, on Uday's team at the fintech office. When Uday became lead in March, he took every hard module himself: the payment engine, the fraud checks, the reconciliation. He said, "If something breaks, I want it to be my mistake."
The rest of us got small tickets. I spent a week changing button colours. Meenakshi, who'd built payment systems before, fixed typos in documentation.
By April Uday was leaving at eleven every night. Code reviews for our small tasks waited days because he had no time. In stand-ups he looked grey.
In May the release date came and went. The payment engine wasn't done. Our manager asked why nobody else had worked on it. Uday said quietly, "I didn't want to risk it."
I can't say exactly what he felt, but he looked like someone who had carried everything and dropped it anyway.

Week one. Chaitanya was made lead of a five-person team building a new booking system. He looked at the list and thought, the search engine and the pricing logic are the hardest. If someone else gets them wrong, I'll look bad. So he took both. Gurleen, who had built pricing logic at her last job, got the login page.
Week four. Chaitanya was at the office past midnight most days. The others finished their small tasks early and waited for his reviews. Gurleen offered twice to help with pricing. "I've got it," he said.
Week eight. Launch week. Search worked; pricing didn't. Gurleen's login page had been finished for a month. The manager postponed the launch by three weeks. In the meeting, Chaitanya stared at the table.
Afterwards Gurleen said gently, "You don't have to carry it all." He nodded, too tired to answer.
